name: The Phoenix Ginkgo

location.address: Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn (Celebrated Tree Walk stop, near the Brown family mausoleum)

access: Free; Green-Wood is open daily (hours at green-wood.com/hours); the Celebrated Trees Walk is on the cemetery's own visitor map
transport: Check route: Green-Wood main entrance at Fifth Ave and 25th St; Sunset Park entrance at 36th St (subway lines and walk times not checked).
story: Twelve ginkgo trees came up from one stump here, and over the years they have grown together into a single tree. Green-Wood Cemetery calls it the Phoenix Ginkgo, and the name does the explaining. Something cut or killed the original tree down to its stump, the stump refused to quit, and the twelve shoots that rose from it have since inosculated, the botanist's word for stems that touch, graft and fuse into one living body. What happened to the first tree, the cemetery does not say, and we will not guess. The story here is the comeback, not the cause. Green-Wood is an accredited arboretum as well as a burial ground, and it puts this tree on its Celebrated Trees walk, printed on its own visitor map in 2023 and again in 2025, near the Brown family mausoleum. Nobody has published a girth or an age, and a tape measure would struggle to say where one stem ends and the next begins. Come in November if you can. Ginkgos turn butter yellow in late autumn and drop their leaves within a day or two, and a dozen fused trunks turning at once is worth the timing. The cemetery is free to enter and open daily, with the hours on its website, and the Celebrated Trees walk is marked on the cemetery's visitor map. If you know when the original tree came down, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the many ginkgo stems, about a dozen, fused together into one tree. It stands on Green-Wood Cemetery's Celebrated Trees walk, near the Brown family mausoleum.

best_time.label: November, when the fused crown turns butter gold

name: The Weeping Beech Tunnel at Green-Wood

location.address: Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn (over Larch Avenue, Celebrated Tree Walk stop)

access: Free; Green-Wood is open daily (hours at green-wood.com/hours); the tunnel is on a cemetery drive and path stop of the owner's Celebrated Trees Walk
transport: Check route: Green-Wood main entrance at Fifth Ave and 25th St; Sunset Park entrance at 36th St (subway lines and walk times not checked)

location_site.name: Weeping beech tunnel on Larch Avenue, Green-Wood

verify_notes: Green-Wood's own visitor map (2023 and 2025 editions) lists 'Weeping Beech Tunnel' as a group of six weeping European beeches whose cascading canopies form a tunnel, a visitor favourite. A Green-Wood tree blog (2009, a blog, a finding aid only) says the most enchanting weeping beech hangs over Larch Avenue and that you must walk or drive under the canopy to go up the road. One compact ensemble with one place to stand (the road under the canopy). Pin: OSM natural=tree node 12609928197 'Weeping Beech' (one point for six trees, so approximate, with a 50 m site). A Brooklyn guide calls it elms; the owner's map and the blog say beech, the owner wins. No planting date, girth or age in any source. Not checked: that the OSM node sits exactly on Larch Avenue (road geometry fetch failed, Overpass at capacity). What tells it apart: the canopy closes over the road.

name: The Blue Atlas Cedars of Queens Botanical Garden

location.address: Queens Botanical Garden, 43-50 Main Street, Flushing, Queens (Main Street entrance, either side of the tree gate sculpture)

access: Garden entry is ticketed or free on some days; check queensbotanical.org for hours and prices before going. The cedars stand at the Main Street entrance (stop #1 on the garden map)
transport: Check route: the 7 train terminates at Flushing-Main St, near the garden (walk time not checked)
verify_notes: The garden's own visitor guide (2016 PDF) says two blue atlas cedars that frame the iconic tree gate sculpture at the Main Street entrance (#1 on the map) are original plantings taken from the 1939 World's Fair 'Gardens on Parade' site, when the garden moved to Main Street in 1961 (Wikipedia gives the move as completed with dedication 19 Oct 1963 and says THREE cedars were transplanted; the owner says two: conflict, kept both counts). Age derived from a documented specimen history: planted for the 1939 fair, so at least 85 years in the ground, possibly older nursery stock; broad range given, no girth recorded. Pin: garden coordinate from Wikipedia (40.7504, -73.8288); the entrance itself was not pinned (Nominatim and Overpass gave no entrance node), so the walker finds it by the tree gate sculpture, not by the coordinate. The garden is a walk-through garden, not a small site, so no location_site. Alive: no dated record of these cedars specifically; the 2016 guide is the latest owner statement, lifecheck RECENT only for the garden area (iNaturalist 2026-10-15). Flagged.
